title: On-carriage & delivery to the consignee
sceneDesc: A landscape from the destination terminal to the consignee's warehouse: road, river and railway. The chosen transport carries the container to the customer.

narration.1: A haulier collects me at {podTerminal} with the pick-up code. At the gate my condition is checked again. How will I travel?
narration.2: Gate-out with the pick-up right; an [[eir]] records my condition. [[on-carriage|On-carriage]] can be [[merchant-haulage]] or [[carrier-haulage]]. Choose the mode. [TO VERIFY:v69]
narration.3: Gate-out ends demurrage and starts import detention; under carrier haulage, the carrier books the slot and the delivery appointment. [TO VERIFY:v21] [TO VERIFY:v70]

1.barge: A barge carries me up the river, then a short truck trip reaches the customer.
1.rail: A train carries me inland, then a truck does the last kilometres.

2.barge: Barge to an inland terminal, then last-mile trucking: cheaper per box over distance, more handlings. [TO VERIFY:v69]
2.rail: Rail shuttle to an inland terminal, then last-mile truck; the detention clock keeps running. [TO VERIFY:v69]
2.*: Road delivery under a [[cmr]] consignment note; road limits apply (e.g. 44 t gross in France). [TO VERIFY:v13]

narration.3: Inland legs share risks with pre-carriage: congestion, weight limits, missed slots. Under carrier haulage, the carrier answers for the inland leg under its B/L terms. [TO VERIFY:v43]

2.reefer: Genset on the road keeps {setPoint}. [TO VERIFY:v57]
2.tank: DG road rules apply (ADR in Europe). [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.oog: Oversize transport may need a permit or escort. [TO VERIFY:v58]
2.*: Import detention runs until the empty is returned. [TO VERIFY:v21]

narration.1: Delivered! The customer checks my seal and signs a delivery receipt.
narration.2: Delivery at {dest} on appointment; the consignee checks the seal and condition and signs the [[pod-proof|proof of delivery]], noting any reservations. [TO VERIFY:v70]
narration.3: Reservations on the POD/CMR preserve claims; a 'clean' signature with visible damage or a wrong seal weakens the consignee's position. [TO VERIFY:v70]
The consignee has no unloading slot for five days. Import detention free time ends in two days. The haulier asks what to do with the loaded container.

text.1: One river barge can carry dozens of containers — taking many trucks off the road. [TO VERIFY:v69]
text.2: Port authorities push barge and rail to reduce road congestion and emissions; modal share targets are set by ports such as HAROPA and Antwerp-Bruges. [TO VERIFY:v69]

body.2: Gate-out EIR records condition; demurrage stops, import detention starts (or combined free time continues). [TO VERIFY:v21]
Import detention runs from full gate-out to empty return at the designated depot. Illustrative: {freeDays} days free. [TO VERIFY:v21] [TO VERIFY:v12]

body.1: The customer checks that my seal is intact and that I'm not damaged, then signs the delivery receipt. Any problem must be written on it.

1.2: The consignee compares the seal number with the B/L before opening the doors.

2.2: Reservations (damage, seal mismatch, shortage) written here preserve the right to claim. [TO VERIFY:v70]

3.2: Signature, date and time close the transport contract for the road leg; the CMR governs international road carriage in Europe. [TO VERIFY:v70]

2.prompt: Why must the consignee check the seal before signing?

options.text: A seal problem noted on the POD preserves the right to claim; a clean signature weakens it

options.fb: The VGM was for loading at origin.

options.text: Because customs requires it for VAT
options.fb: This is about evidence, not VAT.

2.explain: Reservations on delivery documents are the first evidence in any cargo claim. [TO VERIFY:v70]

3.prompt: The seal on arrival is different from the B/L, and the consignee signs a clean POD. What's the consequence?

options.text: The consignee's claim position is weakened; it should have noted a reservation and called a surveyor before unloading
No consequence — the B/L proves the seal
options.fb: The B/L shows what was shipped; the POD shows what was accepted.

options.text: The carrier automatically pays any shortage
options.fb: Liability depends on evidence and the applicable rules.
Not by default; it's a cargo-evidence issue.

3.explain: A seal change may be legitimate (customs inspection) — but only documented reservations allow it to be investigated. [TO VERIFY:v70]

documents: **Release order / pick-up right** — PIN or digital. [TO VERIFY:v68]
**CMR / POD** — signed delivery with reservations. [TO VERIFY:v70]
**Barge or rail consignment note** for intermodal legs.
costs: **On-carriage** — carrier haulage tariff or merchant contract.
**Waiting time** at the consignee beyond free unloading time. [TO VERIFY:v12]
risks: **No delivery slot** → detention and waiting time.
**Overweight on the road** → fines, re-handling. [TO VERIFY:v13]

risks.text: **Genset failure** on the last mile → temperature excursion. [TO VERIFY:v57]

jobs: **Inland / intermodal operations** — carrier haulage at destination.

incoNote.D: Under D-rules, the seller organises this leg; risk passes at the buyer's place (DAP/DDP: ready for unloading; DPU: once unloaded).
incoNote.*: Under {incoterm}, the buyer organises and pays this leg.

1: A truck, train or barge takes me from the port to the customer.
My condition is checked when I leave the port and when I arrive.
The customer signs a delivery receipt and notes any problem.
2: Gate-out ends demurrage; import detention runs until the empty is returned.
Mode choice affects cost, time and handlings.
Reservations on the POD/CMR preserve claims.
3: Plan unloading slots before collecting the box — detention keeps running.
Under carrier haulage, the carrier answers for the inland leg.
Seal mismatches must be documented before unloading.

1.prompt: I'm at the customer's warehouse. What happens next?
1.hint: My job isn't over when I'm empty.

options.text: The customer unloads me, then a truck takes me back — empty — to a depot.
options.confirm: Yes! Once unloaded, I go back to a depot chosen by the carrier, ready for my next trip.

options.text: The customer keeps me as storage.
options.why: I belong to the carrier (or a leasing company).
options.whenRight: If the customer buys or leases the container separately.

options.text: I sail straight back to {pol} full.
options.realLife: Sending cargo back would be a new shipment.
options.whenRight: Only for a return shipment, with a new booking.

2.prompt: Delivered, POD signed. What happens next?

options.text: Unstuffing at the consignee within free time, then the empty is returned to the depot designated by the carrier; import detention stops at empty gate-in.
options.confirm: Correct. The designated return depot matters: returning elsewhere can mean extra charges. [TO VERIFY:v71]

options.text: The empty stays with the consignee to reuse at will.
options.why: Equipment belongs to the carrier and is managed by equipment control.
options.whenRight: With a separate agreement (e.g. street turn or 'triangulation' approved by the carrier).

options.text: Return the empty to the import terminal by default.
options.why: The return location is set by the carrier — often a depot, not the terminal.
options.whenRight: When the carrier designates the terminal as return point.

options.text: Ship the empty back to the origin depot in Asia at the consignee's cost.
options.realLife: The consignee's obligation ends at the designated return depot.

3.prompt: Case: no unloading slot for five days; detention free time ends in two days. What do you advise?

options.text: Inform the consignee of the detention exposure; offer options (drop the loaded box at the haulier's yard or the consignee's site if possible, or accept detention); document the decision.
options.confirm: Right. Detention follows the tariff; transparent options let the cargo side choose the cheapest path. Storage at the haulier's yard has its own costs and security implications. [TO VERIFY:v21] [TO VERIFY:v70]

options.text: Return the loaded box to the terminal to stop detention.
options.why: Re-entering the terminal triggers handling and storage, and detention rules may still apply.
options.realLife: Extra moves and fees, plus a second delivery trip.
options.whenRight: Rarely, if the terminal and carrier agree and it's cheaper.

options.text: Stop the detention clock until the consignee is ready.
options.why: Clock events are defined by the tariff.
options.realLife: An unauthorised stop is a billing error.
options.whenRight: Only with a documented commercial agreement.

options.text: Unload the cargo at the haulier's depot without asking the consignee.
options.why: The consignee decides where its goods are unloaded.
options.realLife: Liability and insurance issues for the haulier.
